The State, represented by the Solicitor, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh ------- Appellant

Divisional Special Judge, Khulna Division and anr ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: In this appeal by special leave the question is whether the High Court Division correctly interpreted section 4(3) vis-a-vis section 10(3) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1958 holding that a Senior Special Judge got no jurisdiction to transfer a case from the court of a Divisional Special Judge. 

 3. Mr. A Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General, has appeared for the State. None has come to oppose him. He has taken us through  relevant provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act including its latest amendments. He has also produced before us copies of certain orders  and notifications of the Government regarding the creation of the courts of Special Judges, including the courts of Divisional Special Judges, along with their territorial jurisdictions. Courts of Special Judges have been created to try cases, ordinarily  known as Anti-Corruption cases, under the  provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act,  1958. Under section 3 thereof "the Government shall  appoint as many Special Judges as may be necessary to try and punish offences specified in the schedules" of this Act. Section 4(2) provides that where there are two or more Special Judges, the Government shall declare one of them to be the "Senior Special Judge" for that "area"-that is, his district/sessions division. By a notification dated 24 October, 1958 the Government declared all Sessions Judges to be the "Ex-officio Senior Special Judges" for their respective "areas" i.e. districts. As to power of taking cognizance of offence triable by Special Judges, originally it was provided that a Special Judge "may take cognizance of any offence". But by Amendment Act No. XIII of 1987, power of taking cognizance of an offence has been given only to the Senior Special Judge in the following words: 

 4. There may be two or more Special Judges in one district (sessions division); such as, the Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge, Assistant Session Judge, Metropolitan Magistrate or some Magistrates of the First Class all of whom have been declared-"Special Judges" by the Government. By a notification dated 4 August, 1979 the Government created four temporary Courts of Special Judges, one at each Divisional Head Quarters namely, Dhaka, Rajshahi, Chittagong and Khulna, and they were given jurisdiction to try Special Cases arising within any district under the respective Divisions. By a subsequent notification dated 9th July 1984 these temporary courts of Special Judges were designated as Courts of "Divisional Special Judges". At that time the Divisional Special Judges were in the rank of Additional Sessions Judges. The Government, by a Notification dated 24th December 1984 gave the Divisional Special Judges the rank and pay of Sessions Judges; but the latter continued as Ex-officio Senior Special Judges with exclusive jurisdiction to take cognizance in all special cases arising in their areas. It is the Senior Special Judges who transfer Special cases to the Divisional Special Judge for disposal. A Divisional Special Judge will not get any cases to try unless they are transferred to him by the Senior Special Judges from their respective districts. As for example, the Divisional Special Judge for Khulna Division will receive and try those cases which are transferred to him by different Senior Special Judges within the Division. A Senior Special Judge, after taking cognizance of an offence in a case, may try it himself or may transfer it to any of the Special Judges, whether the Special Judge is the Divisional Special Judge or he is the Additional Sessions Judge, Assistant Sessions Judge or the Metropolitan Magistrate or a Magistrate First Class-all designated as Special Judges. In other words, as provided in section 4(2), where two or more Special Judges have jurisdiction wholly or partly in the same territorial limits, it is the Senior Special Judge who is the central figure to take cognizance in a case and to transfer it to any of the Special Judges including the Divisional Special Judge. The Divisional Special Judge has been given power to try Special Cases if and when these cases are transferred to him from different districts. A Divisional Special Judge is, therefore, a Special Judge like any other Special Judges, whereas the Sessions Judge is the Ex-officio Senior Special Judge.
